questions.problem:
A function $f(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $11$ | $10.5$ | $6$ | $1.4$ | $-1$ | $-2.5$ |

Approximate ${f}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=-4$ using a forward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation formula

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=-4.$ We choose a step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-4) & ≈\frac{f(-4+2)-f(-4)}{2} \\  & =\frac{f(-2)-f(-4)}{2} \\  & =\frac{10.5-11}{2} \\  & =\frac{-0.5}{2} \\  & =-0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The population of a city is given by the function $n(t),$ where $t$ is the time, in years, from when records first began. The values of $n(t)$, in thousands, for different values of $t$ are given in the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $n(t)$ | $851$ | $856$ | $861$ | $865$ | $870$ |

Approximate the rate of growth in population in the second year $(t=2)$ using a forward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{n}^{′}(t)≈\frac{n(t+h)-n(t)}{h}
$$

 
at the point $t=2.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{n(2+1)-n(2)}{1} \\  & =\frac{n(3)-n(2)}{1} \\  & =\frac{865-861}{1} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So at $t=2$ the rate of growth is approximately $4\,000$ people per year.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $S(m)$ | $90$ | $98$ | $116$ | $130$ | $139$ |

Approximate the rate of growth of the herd at the point where $m=12$ using a forward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{S}^{′}(m)≈\frac{S(m+h)-S(m)}{h},
$$

 
at the point $m=6.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=6.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(12) & ≈\frac{S(12+6)-S(12)}{6} \\  & =\frac{S(18)-S(12)}{6} \\  & =\frac{116-98}{6} \\  & =\frac{18}{6} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, at $m=12$ the rate of growth is approximately $3\,\text{sheep/month}.$

The electrical energy level of a battery powering a house was recorded over time for $10$ hours, starting from time $t=0$ hours. The following table shows the energy level $E(t)$, in kilowatt-hours, recorded at time $t.$

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $E(t)$ | $40$ | $34$ | $29$ | $24$ | $18$ | $12$ |

Approximate the rate of change of energy level at time $t=2$ using a forward difference approximation. Do not round the answer.

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of change is negative if the electrical energy level decreases.

At $t=2,$ the estimated rate of change is {{field-1}} kilowatt-hours per hour.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{E}^{′}(t)≈\frac{E(t+h)-E(t)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=2.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{E(2+2)-E(2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{E(4)-E(2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{29-34}{2} \\  & =\frac{-5}{2} \\  & =-2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, at $t=2$ the rate of change was approximately $-2.5$ kilowatt-hours per hour.

questions.problem:
The weight of a radioactive substance was recorded over time for $15$ seconds. The following table shows the weight $M(t)$, in grams, recorded at time $t$ in seconds.

| $t$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ | $9$ | $12$ | $15$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $M(t)$ | $8.0$ | $7.1$ | $6.3$ | $5.4$ | $4.8$ | $4.1$ |

Approximate the rate of change of weight at time $t=6$ using a forward difference approximation. Do not round the answer.

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of change is negative if the weight decreases.

At $t=6,$ the estimated rate of change is {{field-1}} grams per second.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)≈\frac{M(t+h)-M(t)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=6.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=3.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{′}(6) & ≈\frac{M(6+3)-M(6)}{3} \\  & =\frac{M(9)-M(6)}{3} \\  & =\frac{5.4-6.3}{3} \\  & =\frac{-0.9}{3} \\  & =-0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, at $t=6$ the rate of change was approximately $-0.3$ grams per second.

canonical_examples.problem:
A function $f(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-1.0$ | $-0.7$ | $-0.3$ | $0.7$ | $1.5$ | $2.1$ |

Approximate  at the point $x=3$ using a forward difference approximation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation formula

$$
f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=3.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{f(3+1)-f(3)}{1} \\  & =\frac{f(4)-f(3)}{1} \\  & =\frac{(-0.3)-(-0.7)}{1} \\  & =\frac{0.4}{1} \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The graph of the function $y=g(x)$ is shown below. 
Approximate $g'(x)$ at the point $x=4$ using a forward difference approximation with step size $h=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190413/assets/3084d6ae67f37517f3d8ad0a9a62be05fe1906fcc2a24f69bd29a1e00dfd0373.png)

$$
g'(x) \approx \frac{g(x+h) - g(x)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=4.$  Applying the above formula with $x=4$ and $h=2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(4) & ≈\frac{g(4+2)-g(4)}{2} \\  & =\frac{g(6)-g(4)}{2} \\  & =\frac{2-6}{2} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

Example: 
                    Estimating a Derivative From a Table Using a Forward Difference Approximation: Word Problem
canonical_examples.problem:
The position of a race car along a straight track, measured in feet from the starting line, is given by the function $s(t),$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| $t$ | $0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $0$ | $3$ | $7$ | $12$ | $19$ |

Approximate the velocity $s'(t)$ at the time $t=0.1$ using a forward difference approximation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
s'(t) \approx \frac{s(t+h) - s(t)}{h}
$$

 

at the time $t=0.1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(0.1) & ≈\frac{s(0.1+0.1)-s(0.1)}{0.1} \\  & =\frac{s(0.2)-s(0.1)}{0.1} \\  & =\frac{7-3}{0.1} \\  & =\frac{4}{0.1} \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

So at $t=0.1$ the velocity is approximately $40\, \textrm{ft}/\textrm{s}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
An oil tank has leaked $q(t)$ liters of oil after $t$ hours. The graph of $q(t)$ is shown below. Approximate the rate at which the oil is leaking from the tank when $t=1$ using a forward difference approximation with step size $h=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190413/assets/b6c5286dae7e739a588173bad9c721ae34d07f86e455e44ec9f229628cf54211.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:

$$
q'(t) \approx \frac{q(t+h) - q(t)}{h}
$$

 

at the time $t=1$ with step size $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1+1)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, after $1$ hour, the tank is leaking oil at a rate of approximately $1\,\textrm{liter}/ \textrm{hour}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
For a function $f(x),$ its derivative at a point $x$ is defined by the limit

$$
f'(x) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}.
$$

But often, computing this limit exactly is impossible or impractical. One example might be when we don't have an explicit expression for $f(x).$ In such cases, instead of finding an exact value for $f'(x)$, we can *approximate* the derivative using the formula

 

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of the "step size" $h,$ with $h>0.$

This expression is called the **forward difference approximation** because if $h >0$ then $x+h$ is a step forward (i.e., to the right) from $x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190413/assets/1860d33c3b34fa5c869f5a3c7a04ef4d02271ba30d60f973b892800ef7c9524e.png)

Generally, this and other similar methods are known as **finite-difference** approximations. The smaller the value of $h,$ the better the approximation.
